lessons.title: Lesson 1: Team File Organization and Parts Library
lessons.content:
Welcome to the CAD Setup Guide!

This section will help you navigate your team folders and the VEX parts library to keep your designs organized and efficient.

Locating Your Team Folder

To ensure your work is saved in the correct location, you must navigate through the year-specific directories.

  1. Select the Year: Open the folder labeled 2026-27.
  2. Find Your Team: Within that folder, look for your specific team number, such as 6546A, 6546B, or 6546C.
  3. Save Your Work: Use your designated team folder to organize all of your CAD files throughout the season.

Navigating the VEX EDR Parts Library

Most of your robot's components will be found in the VEX EDR Parts V3 Library.

Library Categories

The library is broken down into several functional categories to help you find parts quickly:

  • Electronics: Motors, sensors, and brains.
  • Motion: Wheels, gears, and sprockets.
  • Screws, Nuts, Standoffs: Essential fasteners.
  • Shafts, Spacers, Bearings: For all rotating assemblies.
  • Structure: The frame and body components of your robot.

Working with Structure

Inside the Structure folder, we primarily focus on Aluminum components because they are the most common parts used in VEX building.

  • Common Pieces: You will frequently use Aluminum 1x1 Angles, 2x2 Angles, and Half-C channels.
  • Core Components: Pay close attention to the 2x C-Channel and 3x C-Channel options, as these are the "backbone" of most robot designs.

quiz.question: When saving your CAD work, where should you navigate first?
options: Any empty folder on the desktop
The year folder (e.g. 2026-27), then your team number
The Electronics category of the parts library
Straight into the VEX EDR Parts V3 Library
quiz.explanation: Go to the year folder (like 2026-27) first, then your team number (e.g. 6546A) so every file stays organized in the right place.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Creating Your Own File
lessons.content:
How to Save a Design in Fusion 360

Saving your work properly keeps your designs organized and accessible from anywhere in the cloud.

Step 1: Check if your file is already named

Look at the top-left corner of Fusion 360.

If it says "Untitled", you need to save it first.

Step 2: Click the Save button

Click the Save icon in the top toolbar, OR press:

  • Mac: Cmd + S
  • Windows: Ctrl + S

Step 3: Name your design

A pop-up will appear. Type a clear name (e.g., Robot Arm V1).

Step 4: Choose where to save

Select the correct Project folder:

VEX → 2026-27 → Team Number

First, navigate to the 2026-27 year folder:

Then, select your team folder (6546A, 6546B, or 6546C) and click Save:

Step 5: Click "Save"

Hit Save. Your design is now stored in the cloud.

After First Save (Important!)

Fusion 360 auto-saves as you work, BUT you should still press Save regularly after big changes.

Common Mistakes to Avoid

  • Forgetting to name your file → hard to find later
  • Not selecting the right project folder
  • Assuming local save → Fusion 360 is cloud-based

quiz.question: How can you tell a Fusion 360 design still needs to be saved for the first time?
quiz.explanation: If the top-left corner shows “Untitled,” the file hasn't been named yet. Hit Save (Cmd+S / Ctrl+S), name it clearly, and pick your team folder.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Component Features
lessons.content:
Fusion 360 Assembly Basics

Save First

Always save your hybrid design before starting.

First Component

Make sure your first component is NOT anchored. You want it free to move.

Modifying Parts

Modify Tool

Use the Modify tool to change the length of:

  • C-channels
  • Standoffs
  • Axles
  • Spacers

Copy & Paste

  • Use if parts are the same length.
  • Avoid if parts need different lengths — changing one changes ALL copies.

Different sizes needed?

Insert a new component from the library.

Connecting Components

Point-to-Point (MOST USED)

  • Connects multiple components
  • Keeps same orientation
  • Best for drivebase

Align Tool

Works on one component only. Changes orientation to match target.

Free Move

Rotate and move parts manually. Good for rough positioning.

Mirroring

Mirror Tool

Duplicates across a plane. Great for symmetrical designs (like drivebases).

Limitations

Does NOT work on:

  • C-channels
  • Spacers
  • Standoffs

Works on:

  • Gears
  • Motors
  • Wheels

quiz.question: Which connection method is recommended for a drivebase because it connects multiple components while keeping the same orientation?
quiz.explanation: Point-to-Point is the go-to joint for drivebases — it connects multiple components and keeps their orientation. Align only works on one component and changes its orientation.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Sample Gear Box
lessons.content:
Materials Used in this Video

Structural Components

  • 2x C-Chan Alu: Two aluminum C-Channels, which serve as the main structural frame to support the gear and wheel assembly.
  • 4x Standoff: Rigid metal spacers used to securely connect and maintain a fixed distance between the two parallel C-Channels.

Motion & Rotation Components

  • 1x LS Shaft: A low-strength (standard square) drive shaft that holds the wheel and rotating components.
  • 2x Bearing Flat, Pillow: Two flat bearing blocks mounted directly to the C-Channels. These support the shaft, allowing it to spin smoothly with minimal friction.

Wheel & Spacing Components

  • 1x 3.25 Omni Wheel: A specialized robotics wheel with small rollers around its circumference, allowing for multi-directional movement.
  • 1x LS Shaft Collar: A locking collar tightened onto the square shaft to prevent it from sliding out of place horizontally.
  • Multiple Spacers (Nylon), .375 OD: Multiple high-durability nylon spacers (with a .375 outer diameter) placed along the shaft to properly align the wheel and prevent it from rubbing against the structural metal.

quiz.question: In the sample gear box, what is the job of the flat pillow bearings mounted to the C-channels?
options: To add weight to the robot
To support the shaft so it spins smoothly with minimal friction
quiz.explanation: Bearings support the drive shaft and let it spin with minimal friction. A shaft collar keeps the shaft from sliding out sideways.

lessons.title: Lesson 1: Gear Ratio
lessons.content:
Mastering Gear Ratios

Gear ratios are one of the most critical design decisions a robotics team must master to optimize the mechanical advantage of their subsystems.

What is a Gear Ratio?

At its core, a gear ratio is the relationship between the rotational speed and force of two or more interlocking (meshing) gears. It compares the input (the gear attached to the motor) to the output (the gear attached to the wheel, arm, or intake).

Because gear teeth are evenly spaced, a gear's diameter is directly proportional to its number of teeth. This allows us to calculate gear ratios simply by counting the teeth:

Gear Ratio = Teeth on Driven Gear (Output)Teeth on Driving Gear (Input) = Driven : Driving

💡 VEX Example: If a small 12-tooth driving gear (connected to a motor) turns a larger 36-tooth driven gear, the calculation is 36 ÷ 12, which simplifies to a 3:1 gear ratio.

The Trade-Off: Speed vs. Torque

The main benefit of changing gear ratios is the ability to customize a mechanism for either Speed or Torque (rotational force). However, these two traits have an inverse relationship — you cannot increase one without decreasing the other.

1. Geared for Torque (Mechanical Advantage)

  • Setup: A smaller gear drives a larger gear (e.g., 12-tooth driving a 36-tooth).
  • The Result: The output shaft has 3x the torque, but only 1/3 of the speed.
  • Best used for: Lifting heavy robot arms, closing high-pressure claws, or building high-traction drivetrains designed to push other robots.

2. Geared for Speed

  • Setup: A larger gear drives a smaller gear (e.g., 36-tooth driving a 12-tooth).
  • The Result: The output shaft has 3x the speed, but only 1/3 of the torque.
  • Best used for: Intakes that need to grab objects quickly or high-speed flywheels for launching game elements.

📙 [Advanced] VEX Mechanical Lessons Day 1

quiz.question: A 12-tooth driving gear (on the motor) turns a 36-tooth driven gear. What is the gear ratio?
quiz.explanation: Gear ratio = driven teeth ÷ driving teeth = 36 ÷ 12 = 3:1. A larger driven gear gives more torque but less speed.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Drivetrain Types
lessons.content:
Drivetrain Types

VEX drivetrains come in many flavors. The Purdue SIGBots Wiki has a great overview — give it a read:

📖 Drivetrains | Purdue SIGBots Wiki

Summary of the Drivetrains Overview

  • Definition: VEX drivetrains are assemblies — typically made of wheels — used by robots to navigate and traverse the VRC (VEX Robotics Competition) field.
  • Trade-offs: Every drivetrain style comes with its own unique set of advantages and disadvantages depending on the game's requirements.

The 4 Most Common Types

  1. Tank Drive
  2. Mecanum Drive
  3. X-Drive
  4. H-Drive

quiz.question: Which of these is NOT one of the four most common VEX drivetrain types?
quiz.explanation: The four common types are Tank, Mecanum, X-Drive, and H-Drive. “Helicopter Drive” isn't a thing!

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Example Drivetrain
lessons.content:
🟩 What TO Include in the CAD

These are the essential structural and mechanical components that define the physical footprint, geometry, and spacing of your drivetrain:

  • Chassis Structure: All aluminum C-channels and angles that make up the primary frame.
  • Wheels: The exact wheel types (e.g., 2.75 AS Omni wheels) positioned precisely to determine ground clearance and track width.
  • Motors: The motor cartridges and housings to ensure there is physical clearance for them and they don't collide with the frame.
  • Gears: The main driving and driven gears (e.g., 48T HS Gear) along with their specific high-strength center inserts to establish exact gear spacing and center-to-center distances.

🟥 What NOT to Include in the CAD

These items are intentionally omitted to keep your assembly file lightweight, prevent software lag in Autodesk Inventor, and avoid cluttering your browser tree with hundreds of unnecessary constraints:

  • Fasteners (Screws, Nuts, & Rivets): Typically omitted at this stage. Including every single nut and bolt adds massive computational overhead for zero design benefit.
  • Wiring & Electronics Cables: Omitted because flexible wires do not affect physical spacing or structural integrity.
  • Flexible Materials: Rubber bands, latex tubing, and pneumatic lines are excluded because they are difficult to model statically and are better managed during the physical build.

🟧 Optional

  • Shaft Collars & Spacers: Not necessary. Do not waste time constraining every plastic spacer or metal shaft collar, as they do not alter the main structural layout.
  • Screw Joints

quiz.question: Which parts should you always include when CADing a drivetrain?
options: Every single screw, nut, and rivet
All the wiring and rubber bands
quiz.explanation: Include the structural parts that define spacing and geometry (C-channels, wheels, motors, gears). Skip fasteners, wiring, and flexible parts to keep the file light.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Building Your First Drivebase
lessons.content:
Your First Drivebase

Watch the walkthrough above, then build along. This is the example drivebase referenced in the team's video lesson plan file — and other drivebase examples are available in that same file if you want to compare options.

🧩 Parts You Will Need

To CAD this drivebase, grab the following parts from the library:

  • C-Channels — the aluminum frame that everything mounts to
  • Wheels — what your robot rolls on
  • Gears — to transfer power from the motors to the wheels
  • Motors — the V5 motors that drive the gears
  • Standoffs — to space and connect channels structurally
  • Spacers — to position parts correctly along the shafts

⏱️ Keep It Simple — Save Time

You do not have to add every shaft collar or fuss over exact spacing in the CAD. The mechanical team will figure that out during the physical build.

The goal here is to lay out the core structure quickly so the team can focus more on scoring mechanisms — that's where matches are won. A drivebase just needs to be solid and roll well; don't burn hours constraining tiny plastic spacers.

✅ Worth CADing⏭️ Skip for now
C-channels (the frame)Every shaft collar
Wheels in their real positionsExact spacer-by-spacer spacing
Motors & gears (for clearance & spacing)Screws, nuts, and rivets
Standoffs that define structureWires and rubber bands

Recap

  • Gather: C-channels, wheels, gears, motors, standoffs, spacers.
  • Don't sweat shaft collars and precise spacing — the mechanical team handles that on the real robot.
  • Build fast so the team can spend its energy on scoring.
  • This example, plus other drivebase examples, lives in the video lesson plan file.

quiz.question: According to this lesson, what should you NOT waste time on when CADing your first drivebase?
options: Every shaft collar and exact spacing — the mechanical team figures that out
quiz.explanation: Don't fuss over every shaft collar or exact spacing — the mechanical team sorts that out on the real build. Lay out the core structure fast so the team can focus on scoring.

lessons.title: Lesson 1: Triangle Bracing
lessons.content:
Why It Is Important

  • Eliminates Mechanical Slop: Even if you tighten screws and nuts perfectly, the slight tolerances (wiggle room) in structural metal holes will cause a chassis to warp over time. A diagonal brace locks the geometry in place.
  • Distributes Stress Evenly: When a force is applied to one corner of a robot (for example, hitting a wall or lifting a heavy game element), a triangle brace redirects that pushing or pulling force along the axis of the diagonal beam, spreading the load throughout the entire chassis rather than concentrating it on a single weak joint.
  • Prevents High-Torque Warping: High-torque subsystems — like a heavy lifting arm or a high-velocity flywheel — exert massive counter-forces on the robot's base. Without triangular support, the frame can twist, causing gears to misalign, axles to bind, and motors to stall.

Why People Should Use It in Robotics

  • Drastically Increases Build Reliability: A robot built with triangle bracing will maintain its square alignment throughout a long tournament. This means your autonomous routines will be more consistent because the chassis isn't slightly warping between matches.
  • Saves Weight Compared to "Over-building": Instead of adding multiple heavy layers of thick metal channels to make a robot rigid, a single, strategically placed diagonal gusset or thin bar creates the same structural integrity at a fraction of the weight.

quiz.question: Why is triangle (diagonal) bracing important on a robot chassis?
options: It makes the robot heavier on purpose
It replaces the need for motors
It locks the geometry in place and stops the frame from warping or twisting
It only makes the robot look cooler
quiz.explanation: A diagonal brace turns a wobbly rectangle into rigid triangles, removing slop and preventing high-torque warping that would misalign gears and axles.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Weight Saving
lessons.content:
1. Material Selection

  • Aluminum over Steel: Replace all steel C-channels and plates with their aluminum counterparts, which are significantly lighter.
  • NEVER USE STEEL
  • Polycarbonate/Lexan: Use polycarbonate panels for non-load-bearing parts. You can use the "Voronoi" technique (cutting geometric triangles out of plastic sheets) to remove excess weight while maintaining structural rigidity. [1, 2, 3]

2. Fastener Optimization

  • Nylon Hardware: Swap heavy steel nuts for nylon locking nuts where load-bearing is minimal.
  • Zip Ties: In areas experiencing only tensile forces (not compression or torsion), use zip ties instead of metal C-channels.
  • Shorter Bolts: Cut down long bolts or use the shortest screw possible to avoid extra metal protruding.
  • Thumb Screws: Use legal thumb screws (the only legal nylon screw) where applicable. [1, 2]

3. Structural Design

  • Minimize Profiles: Replace 3-wide or 5-wide C-channel with lighter 2-wide C-channel.
  • Half-Cuts: Utilize half-cut C-channel for sections that don't need full-length metal. Use standoffs to make up for the required space.
  • Trussing: Drill patterns of holes in larger pieces of metal (without compromising structural integrity) to remove excess mass. [1]

4. Motion & Drivetrain

  • Shafts vs. Collars: Use standoffs and locking collars made of aluminum.
  • Wheel Choice: Opt for smaller and lighter wheels, like 2.75" omni wheels, rather than heavier alternatives.
  • Limit Drivetrain Weight: The drivetrain is the last place you should cut weight. Keep heavy motors and structural metal at the base to maintain a low center of gravity. [1, 2, 3]

quiz.question: Which material should you use for C-channels to save weight?
quiz.explanation: Aluminum is far lighter than steel — the lesson says NEVER use steel. Polycarbonate/Lexan is great for non-load-bearing parts too.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: C Channels vs L Channels
lessons.content:
Channel TypeRelative WeightTorsional (Twist) ResistancePrimary Use Case
C-ChannelHeavyExcellentMain chassis rails, lift arms, heavy load-bearing frames.
Thick L-ChannelMediumModerateHigh-torque joint reinforcement, compact high-stress bracing.
Normal L-ChannelLightLowLight corner ties, sensor mounts, intake guides.

1. C-Channels vs. L-Channels

  • C-Channels: These have a flat back (web) and two side flanges, forming a "C" or "U" shape. They offer the highest structural strength and excellent resistance to both bending and twisting (torsional stress). They are the go-to choice for robot chassis frames, lift towers, and heavy-duty mechanisms.
  • L-Channels (Angles): These have only two legs meeting at a 90-degree angle. They lack the second side flange of a C-channel, making them much lighter and more compact. They are primarily used for cross-bracing, intake structures, or guard rails where saving space and weight is critical.

2. L-Channels Comparison

Normal (Standard) L-Channel

  • Weight: Very lightweight, helping keep the robot's center of gravity low or reducing the load on motorized joints.
  • Flexibility: It has a tendency to flex or twist if placed under heavy structural stress, high torque, or impacts from other robots.
  • Best Used For: Low-stress components, alignment guides, mounting sensors, or acting as simple structural ties.

Thick L-Channel

  • Strength & Durability: Provides significantly higher resistance to bending, shearing, and hole-deformation (where screws wallow out the metal holes under high stress).
  • Weight Penalty: Heavier than the normal version, meaning it should be used strategically to avoid making a mechanism sluggish.
  • Best Used For: High-stress pivot points, cross-braces directly subjected to motor torque, or external bumpers meant to absorb heavy impacts.

quiz.question: Compared to an L-channel, a C-channel is generally…
options: Heavier, but with excellent resistance to bending and twisting
quiz.explanation: A C-channel's flat back plus two flanges give the highest strength and torsional resistance — great for chassis rails and lift arms. L-channels are lighter but weaker, used for bracing and mounts.
